# Assignment 1. Handwritten digit recognition with K-nearest neighbors

The data file `optdigits.csv` contains information about normalized bitmaps of
handwritten digits, each column representing a pixel in an 8x8 image as an
integer in the range from 0 to 16, with the last column containing the actual
digit. We first loaded the file as a data.frame `digits`.

```{r a1-data}
library(kknn)

# optdigits.csv has no header: 64 pixel columns + last column = digit (0-9)
digits <- read.csv("data/optdigits.csv", header = FALSE)
colnames(digits)[ncol(digits)] <- "digit"
digits$digit <- as.factor(digits$digit)
```

## 1. Data partitioning

```{r a1-split}
n <- dim(digits)[1]
set.seed(12345)
id_train <- sample(1:n, floor(n * 0.5))
train <- digits[id_train,]

id_tmp <- setdiff(1:n, id_train)
set.seed(12345)
id_valid <- sample(id_tmp, floor(n * 0.25))
valid <- digits[id_valid,]

id_test <- setdiff(id_tmp, id_valid)
test <- digits[id_test,]
```

The data.frame `digits` was then split into the following data.frames randomly:

- 50% `train`: 1911 rows
- 25% `valid`: 955 rows
- 25% `test`: 957 rows

For this, we used the code from Lecture 1a ("Holdout in R") and we set a seed
with `set.seed(12345)`.

## 2. 30-nearest neighbor classifier

```{r a1-knn30}
# Fits models
fit_train <- kknn(
  digit ~ ., train = train, test = train, k = 30, kernel = "rectangular"
)
fit_test <- kknn(
  digit ~ ., train = train, test = test, k = 30, kernel = "rectangular"
)
```

```{r a1-knn30-errors}
# Gets confusion matrices
cm_train <- table(True = train$digit, Predicted = fit_train$fitted.values)
cm_test <- table(True = test$digit, Predicted = fit_test$fitted.values)

# Defines missclass function to calculate classification error
missclass <- function(true, predicted) {
  n <- length(true)
  1 - sum(diag(table(true, predicted))) / n
}

# Defines digit_missclass function to get each digit's classification error
digit_missclass <- function(true, predicted) {
  1 - diag(table(true, predicted)) / rowSums(table(true, predicted))
}

# Shows the error per digit and overall, for training and test data
error_table <- rbind(
  Training = c(
    digit_missclass(train$digit, fit_train$fitted.values),
    All = missclass(train$digit, fit_train$fitted.values)
  ),
  Test = c(
    digit_missclass(test$digit, fit_test$fitted.values),
    All = missclass(test$digit, fit_test$fitted.values)
  )
)
knitr::kable(
  error_table, digits = 3, format.args = list(nsmall = 3),
  caption = "Misclassification error per digit and overall (k = 30)."
)
```

As expected, we observe the train misclassification error (`0.045`) is smaller
than the test misclassification error (`0.053`). The train error is
slightly smaller as it is calculated on the same data that is used in the
KNN model. This small gap shows little overfitting.

The digit `0` has the lowest train error at `0.000` and the third lowest test
error at `0.013` after the digits `6` and `7`. The digit `6` has the lowest
test error at `0.000` and is tied for the second lowest train error at `0.010`
with the digit `2`. This tells us that these digits are the easiest ones to
recognize in this handwritten set, considering its low resolution.

On the other hand, the digit `4` has the highest train error at `0.091` and the
highest test error at `0.138`, followed by `8` at `0.103`, and `5` at `0.097`.
The digit `4` is thus the hardest one to recognize in this dataset.

<!-- Narrower table columns so both confusion matrices fit side by side -->
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}

```{r a1-confusion}
# Shows the confusion matrices side by side
# (rows: true digit, columns: predicted digit).
# The two LaTeX commands centre the tables and leave a 1 cm gap between them
knitr::kables(
  list(
    "\\centering",
    knitr::kable(cm_train),
    "\\hspace{1cm}",
    knitr::kable(cm_test)
  ),
  caption = paste(
    "Confusion matrices for the 30-nearest neighbour classifier:",
    "train (left) and test (right).",
    "Rows are the true digits, columns the predicted digits."
  )
)
```

\setlength{\tabcolsep}{6pt}

Looking at the confusion matrices, the diagonals tell us most samples are
correctly classified as expected. Every other cell outside the main diagonal
contains the samples that were incorrectly classified. On the train data we can
see the most common error was the digit `1` being misclassified as `2`, followed
closely by `8` as `1`, which is the most common error on the test data. This
could be due to the dataset's low resolution which does not allow the `8`'s
details in the middle to be displayed clearly. Other common mistakes are
misclassifying the digit `4` as `7` or the digit `5` as `9`. A higher resolution
dataset may decrease the incidence of these errors.

In conclusion, the 30-NN classifier does a good overall job for this dataset,
with a test accuracy of `94.7%`.


## 3. Easiest and hardest cases of digit "8"

```{r a1-digit8, fig.show="hold", out.width="19%", fig.width=4, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="The two easiest (left) and three hardest (right) cases of digit 8 in the training data. p is the predicted probability of the correct class."}
# Gets the predicted probabilities for the digit 8
idx_8 <- which(train$digit == "8")
prob_8 <- fit_train$prob[idx_8, "8"]

# Gets the 2 samples of 8 with the highest probability and the 3 with the lowest
easiest <- idx_8[order(prob_8, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]]
hardest <- idx_8[order(prob_8)[1:3]]

# Reshapes one training row into the 8x8 image (pixels are stored row by row)
plot_digit <- function(i, title) {
  img <- matrix(as.numeric(train[i, 1:64]), nrow = 8, byrow = TRUE)
  # heatmap() draws row 1 at the bottom, so reverse the rows to show the
  # digit upright; scale = "none" keeps the raw pixel counts
  heatmap(
    img[8:1,], Colv = NA, Rowv = NA, scale = "none", labRow = NA, labCol = NA,
    main = title, col = grey(seq(1, 0, length.out = 17)),
    # The frame keeps all five images at the same scale in the PDF
    add.expr = box(col = "grey60")
  )
}

for (i in easiest) {
  plot_digit(i, sprintf("Easy: p = %.2f", fit_train$prob[i, "8"]))
}
for (i in hardest) {
  plot_digit(i, sprintf("Hard: p = %.2f", fit_train$prob[i, "8"]))
}
```

Here are the two easiest and the three hardest cases for the digit `8`, that is
the two with the highest predicted probability and the three with the lowest.
With the data resolution, we can clearly see the first two are the digit `8`,
while the last three could be easily mistaken for other digits as the
characteristic round figures from the digit `8` cannot be observed. These could
be easily mistaken as `1` or `6` or some other digit.

In the 64-dimensional space of our features, these cases are not spatially close
to the other samples of the digit `8`, and therefore their predicted probability
of being `8` is low. Most of their 30 closest neighbors in this space belong to
other classes.


## 4. Misclassification error for K = 1, ..., 30

```{r a1-misclass}
get_knn_missclass_error <- function(train, valid, k) {
  # Fits models
  fit_train <- kknn(
    digit ~ ., train = train, test = train, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
  )
  fit_valid <- kknn(
    digit ~ ., train = train, test = valid, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
  )

  # Calculates train and validation error rates
  error_train <- missclass(train$digit, fit_train$fitted.values)
  error_valid <- missclass(valid$digit, fit_valid$fitted.values)

  c(error_train = error_train, error_valid = error_valid)
}

# Calculates errors for each value of k from 1 to 30
errors <- sapply(1:30, function(k) get_knn_missclass_error(train, valid, k))
```

```{r a1-misclass-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Training and validation misclassification error for k = 1, ..., 30."}
k_values <- 1:30
k_opt <- which.min(errors["error_valid",])
col_train <- "#2a78d6"  # blue
col_valid <- "#eb6834"  # orange

# Plots an empty plot first so the grid and the k marker sit behind the lines
plot(
  k_values, errors["error_train",], type = "n", xaxt = "n",
  xlim = c(1, 34), ylim = c(0, max(errors)), las = 1, bty = "l",
  xlab = "k (number of neighbours)", ylab = "Misclassification error"
)
axis(1, at = c(1, seq(5, 30, by = 5)))
abline(h = axTicks(2), col = "grey90")
abline(v = k_opt, lty = 2, col = "grey50")

# Adds lines with train and validation errors
lines(
  k_values, errors["error_train",], type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
  lwd = 2, col = col_train
)
lines(
  k_values, errors["error_valid",], type = "o", pch = 17, cex = 0.8,
  lwd = 2, col = col_valid
)

# Labels at the right end of each line, and the optimal K
text(30, errors[, 30], c("Training", "Validation"), pos = 4, cex = 0.85)
text(
  k_opt, max(errors), paste("optimal k =", k_opt), pos = 4, cex = 0.85,
  col = "grey30"
)
legend(
  "bottomright", legend = c("Training", "Validation"),
  col = c(col_train, col_valid), pch = c(19, 17), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
  )
```

Figure 2 shows a small `k` returns a more flexible and complex model, while a
large `k` produces a smoother and simpler model. The misclassification errors
mostly increase as `k` increases. It is self-evident that using `k=1` returns an
error of `0` on the training data as each observation is its own prediction. For
the validation set, the error first decreases and is minimized at `k=3` and
`k=4`. We are using `k=3` as it is the first one.

```{r a1-misclass-optimal}
# Sets the optimal value of k
k <- 3

# Fits a new model to get the test error
fit_test <- kknn(
  digit ~ ., train = train, test = test, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
)

# Gets train and valid results
errors <- get_knn_missclass_error(train, valid, k)

# Shows the training, validation and test errors for the optimal k
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Training = errors["error_train"],
    Validation = errors["error_valid"],
    Test = missclass(test$digit, fit_test$fitted.values)
  ),
  digits = 4, format.args = list(nsmall = 4), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste0(
    "Misclassification errors for the optimal k (k = ", k, ")."
  )
)
```

For our chosen 3-NN model, the test error is equal to `0.0240` (`97.6%`
accuracy), which is very close to the validation error of `0.0251`, so the
validation set was a good guide. Both of these values are considerably larger
than the train error of `0.0115`, which suggests some overfitting. Figure 2
shows that at `k=7` both error lines are closest to each other, however the
validation error is higher at that point. Overall, the 3-NN model has less than
half the test error of the 30-NN model (`0.053`).


## 5. Cross-entropy for K = 1, ..., 30

```{r a1-crossentropy}
get_knn_cross_entropy <- function(train, valid, k) {
  fit_valid <- kknn(
    digit ~ ., train = train, test = valid, k = k, kernel = "rectangular"
  )
  prob <- fit_valid$prob

  # Indicator matrix I(Y_i = C_m): one row per observation, one column per digit
  Y <- outer(valid$digit, colnames(prob), "==")

  # Cross-entropy as on Lecture 1a, slide 27 (1e-15 avoids log(0))
  -sum(Y * log(prob + 1e-15))
}

cross_entropy <- sapply(
  1:30, function(k) get_knn_cross_entropy(train, valid, k)
)
```

```{r a1-crossentropy-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Validation cross-entropy for k = 1, ..., 30."}
k_values <- 1:30
k_opt_ce <- which.min(cross_entropy)
col_valid <- "#eb6834"  # orange, as the validation line in the Task 4 plot

# Plots an empty plot first so the grid and the k marker sit behind the line
plot(
  k_values, cross_entropy, type = "n", xaxt = "n",
  ylim = c(0, max(cross_entropy)), las = 1, bty = "l",
  xlab = "k (number of neighbours)", ylab = "Validation cross-entropy"
)
axis(1, at = c(1, seq(5, 30, by = 5)))
abline(h = axTicks(2), col = "grey90")
abline(v = k_opt_ce, lty = 2, col = "grey50")

# Adds the validation cross-entropy line
lines(
  k_values, cross_entropy, type = "o", pch = 17, cex = 0.8,
  lwd = 2, col = col_valid
)

# Marks the optimal k
text(
  k_opt_ce, max(cross_entropy), paste("optimal k =", k_opt_ce),
  pos = 4, cex = 0.85, col = "grey30"
)
```

Figure 3 shows the validation cross-entropy at different values of `k`. Here, we
observe that the optimal value is `k=6`. We can observe that for small values of
`k` the cross-entropy is the highest. At `k=1` every misclassified sample gets
a probability `0` which adds $-log(1\times10^{-15})\approx34.5$ to the sum.

Using the cross-entropy may suit a multinomial response better because it is the
minus log-likelihood of the multinomial model. It also uses the predicted
probabilities instead of only using the predicted class. Thus, it rewards the
model's confidence in its correct predictions and penalizes its confident
incorrect predictions as well.
